ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: wishes and promises
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How wishes work, and what granting, promising, refusing and ignoring do.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Don't promise a bed you don't have the wood for.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists make wishes that fit their situation, their traits and what the colony can actually build. Each wish has a deadline, and the council can answer it in four ways. The page "what colonists wish for" lists every kind of wish and when it comes up.

li.heading: The four answers

table.li: Answer | What happens

Grant | The colonist is pleased, trusts the council more and is always motivated (faster work for a few days), more so if the wish was promised. The happier they already are, the more likely the wish also brings an inspiration: creativity, a work or shooting frenzy, recruiting, surgery.

Promise | The deadline moves out by half the remaining time plus two days, and the colonist gains +4 trust right away. Some wishes are acted on as soon as you promise them: promising a party calls one, and promising a hunt marks the prey. A broken promise costs far more than an ordinary lapse.
Refuse | It costs a little now, and then it's settled. A refusal costs less than letting the wish lapse.

Let it lapse | The colonist takes it badly. Colonists who run out of patience sometimes do it themselves: they plan the lamp, take the bed or set their own work priorities, and trust the council less for it.

li.after: Promise only what you'll actually do in time, and refuse what you won't do.

li.heading: The rest of the colony
li.text: Other colonists react too: friends are happy for them, and some object openly. Someone with a request of their own still waiting only feels passed over ("the favorite") when the same colonist has had a second wish granted since their own last one, within 30 days; a single wish granted is just good news. Watch for wishes that come with objections, since granting them pleases one colonist and annoys another.

li.heading: Beliefs and diets
li.text: Nobody asks for what their own beliefs forbid. A couple whose ideoligion keeps lovin for the married doesn't ask to share a bed before the wedding; an engaged couple asks for the wedding instead, and more often. A vegetarian doesn't ask for a smokehouse, a grill or a hunt; a teetotaler, or an ideoligion that keeps drugs to medicine, never asks for beer or a brewery; an addict being kept off their drug by the drug policy doesn't ask for a supply of it; a nudist doesn't ask for clothes; an ideoligion that prefers darkness doesn't ask for a lamp, and one that prefers darklight asks for a dark torch. The same goes for the other precepts of the game's Ideology, Vanilla Ideology Expanded - Memes and Alpha Memes: fishing, travel, fire, books, pets, private rooms, armour, prosthetics, a biosculpter, a woodpile from felled trees, executions. Wishes for food count only what the colonist may eat: fine meals without meat for a vegetarian, and for someone whose ideoligion holds both of Alpha Memes' required diets, only fungus, insect meat or meals with some of either. If their beliefs change while a wish is open (a conversion, a reformed ideoligion), the wish is let go quietly with no blame, and a granted one they can no longer keep, like a shared bed under a new ideoligion, stops being watched. Life goals and council projects follow the same rules.

li.heading: Taking it back
li.text:
Some wishes give something that stays: a bed kept for guests, a room of their own, a nicer or roomier bedroom, a bed shared with a partner, a workshop or other room for their passion, a telescope, a tool cabinet, a sauna, a pen for the animals, a real floor, a stocked infirmary, a pet, the work they love switched on, hours of rest in their schedule, a decree they asked for. For about 60 days after it's granted (90 for rooms), the council is watched on it. After that the colony has lived with it, and changing it is just life. The Wishes page lists what's being watched, and whether it's kept, missing or taken back.
One-offs aren't watched: a party, a feast, a hunt, a birthday, a visit, a lesson, a journey. Neither are clothes and weapons, which wear out, nor stores that are there to be eaten or burned, like firewood or hay.

table.li: When | What happens
It goes missing | You get a message at once, naming who and what. A grace period starts: a day by default (the setting can make it none, half a day or three days).

It's being moved | Not missing at all: a building packed up to be carried, stored or reinstalled, a plan or frame of the same thing being built where it belongs (for up to a week), or a bed lent to a patient.
Back within the grace | Nothing happens.

Still gone after it | "They took back what the council gave me": a bad mood of 3 to 6 for 5 days, the bigger the sooner it happened, and stronger for those with high standards. Trust drops as for a broken promise, a line goes in their journal, and their partner and close friends trust the council a little less. They may ask for it again soon.
Back within 5 days of that | The council made it right: the bad mood ends, half the trust comes back, and they feel grateful (a feeling, not a mood).

li.after: A fire, a raid or a collapse isn't the council's doing: a building lost that way ends the watch quietly, and for two days after a raid nothing counts as missing, so there's time to rebuild. Stores meant to be used only need to stay partly stocked: a third of the medicine or healroot asked for, half the silver or books. Things in their own room are watched only while they have a room; losing the room is the room's own wish.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: trust in the council
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Bitter to devoted: what trust does to mood, work and loyalty.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Answer every wish, even when the answer is no.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every colonist has a level of trust in the council: bitter, doubtful, neutral, trusting or devoted. It rises with granted wishes, kept promises and heeded petitions, falls with lapses, refusals and broken promises, and slowly drifts back toward neutral. Living under a decree they hate wears it down day by day; one they love builds it. Trust shows on the Wishes page, with its history in the tooltip.

li.heading: What it changes
li.text:
Trusting and devoted colonists work and learn faster and have fewer mental breaks; the Health tab shows this as "loyal to the council". Doubtful and bitter colonists work slower and break sooner ("grudge against the council"). Trusting colonists are also more patient with their wishes, and bitter ones less so.
Check the trust list before big decisions. It tells you who can take a disappointment and who can't.

li.heading: When someone wants to leave
li.text:
On Demanding stakes, a colonist who stays bitter for days may announce they're leaving, and walk out three days later unless their trust recovers. Children, anyone whose partner stays, and colonies of fewer than four never lose someone this way.
Granting one of their wishes or keeping a promise to them is usually enough to make them stay.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: rising standards
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Why a happy colony gets harder to please, and how to bring its standards back down.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Feed them fine meals for a season and they'll start complaining about simple ones.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
While a colonist is happy, their standards creep up from modest to comfortable, particular and spoiled. High standards make the council's rewards count for less, its letdowns hurt more, and the game's own comforts count for less. Hard times bring them back down, and so does the austerity decree.
None of this takes anything away. A colony that lives well still feels it; it just doesn't float at the top of the mood bar on a pile of small pleasures. A life goal reached is the exception to everything on this page: it counts in full, whatever their standards and however good life already is.

li.heading: How they move

table.li: Mood | Standards
Above 85% | Rise faster
About 70% to 85% | Rise
40% to about 70% | Fall slowly
Below 40% | Fall
Under austerity | Fall quickly

li.after: Ascetics barely rise; the greedy and jealous rise faster. Feasts, festivals and bonfires raise everyone's standards a little.

li.heading: Spoiled colonists
li.text: A spoiled colonist gets half the mood from the council's rewards and about 40% more from its letdowns. They're less patient, make wishes more often, reach for luxuries, and ask for more: two impressiveness levels instead of one, fine meals instead of simple ones.

li.heading: The game's comforts
li.text: Standards also reach the good moods that come from the base game and your other mods: a fine meal, an impressive bedroom, a party, a good joy activity.

table.li: Standards | Good moods from the game and other mods
Modest | In full
Comfortable | 90%
Particular | 80%
Spoiled | 70%

li.after: Only the first 10 points of each mood count for less: a +5 fine meal is +4 for a particular colonist, and a +40 catharsis is still +37 for a spoiled one. Bad moods are never touched, and Rimfolk's own good moods already follow standards, so they aren't shrunk twice. Hover a good mood in the Needs tab to see what it would be without standards. This needs the deeper game hooks; the "Standards cover the game's comforts" setting turns it off.

li.heading: When life is good
li.text:
Someone whose life is already good gets used to good things faster. When a colonist's mood is above 75%, a new good memory from Rimfolk fades sooner, smoothly down to half its usual time from 90% mood. It feels just as good while it lasts, and in hard times good things last their full length, so a lift after a bad stretch stays with them. A life goal reached always lasts its full time. A good memory about someone keeps its effect on opinion for the full time; only the mood ends sooner.
The "Good times" line in a colonist's Mood tab says what these rules take off right now. Each has its own setting.

li.heading: Good moods add up slowly
li.text: Every good mood Rimfolk gives shares one budget, from a wish granted to a reunion: the biggest count in full and the rest for less, by their place among the good moods on the colonist's mind.

table.li: Place, biggest first | Counts for
First and second | In full
Third | 60%
Fourth | 45%
Fifth | 35%
Sixth and after | A quarter

li.after: Nothing is hidden: every good mood stays on the Needs tab at what it counts for now, so a +3 deep in the pile still shows as +1, and its tooltip says "+0.8 instead of +3". Bad moods, the good moods of the game and other mods, and a life goal reached aren't part of it. The "Good moods add up slowly" setting turns this off.

li.heading: Good moments that aren't moods
li.text: Not every good moment lifts a mood. Rimfolk keeps mood for the moments that matter: weddings, wishes granted, reunions, victories, recoveries, life goals reached, the end of a personal story, real celebrations and grief shared. About half of its small good moments (248 of 474) give something that fits instead, and still show as a speech bubble, a line in the social log or the news, or a line in the journal.

table.li: Instead of mood | For example
Opinion only | A good talk, a friendly disagreement, a wound patched up: they think better of each other, and nobody's mood moves.
Recreation | A joke at work, dice with a traveler, snow falling, birdsong, a herd going by, music in the air.
Rest or comfort | A sweet dream, sleeping late, a friend covering a shift; a dry roof, a trick against the cold, a proper wash.
Practice | Talking shop in a passion they share, a child learning from a grown-up, sparring forms, calming an animal in a storm.
A rare inspiration | A strange dream, a great beast at the tree line, a falling star, a little magic.
A feeling | Awe at the lightning tree, pride in the pilgrims fed, relief at the thaw, fellowship after having their say at a meeting, gratitude for a decree they asked for.
Trust in the council | Seeing a dilemma handled fairly, spoils shared out evenly, the council's precautions.
The road's gifts | A little research from a traveler's star names or books, and a little goodwill after tea with a trader or water for a wounded raider.
Only the journal | The smallest touches: lights over the marsh, a shape in the fog, a stolen dinner.

li.after: These follow the reward strength setting and standards, like the moods they replace, and give nothing on "Advisor only". The heart still feels them at their old size, so feelings, belonging and the strain friends ease work as before. A small line of floating text over the colonist says what they got ("+ recreation"), while colonists' speech shows at all.

li.heading: Bringing them down
li.text: If the whole colony is particular or spoiled, a week of austerity resets expectations cheaply. You also don't have to hold every celebration: turning down a feast or a festival now and then keeps standards from climbing.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: decrees
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Policies that trade mood for output: long hours, rationing, drills and more.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Call long hours while the colony is happy, not once it's already miserable.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The Decrees page puts policies in force for a few days: up to two at once, each with a cooldown afterward. Each trades mood (and sometimes trust) for something the colony needs, or, like festival days and days of mourning, the other way around. The page shows who will love or hate each one before you decide, with a bar of how the colony stands on it. The decrees stand in their kinds (work, food and stores, order and health, rest and spirit, faith, the wider world), each kind foldable; filters show only those ready now, in force, asked for, needed now or waiting; the order can be by kind, most wanted first or soonest ready; and "At a glance" above the cards shows every decree as a chip with its support bar, a click going to its card.

li.heading: The decrees

table.li: Decree | What it does
Long hours | Work 15% faster.
Rationing | Hunger 25% slower.
Drills | Everyone who can fight trains shooting and melee every waking hour.
Study hours | Learning 30% and research 20% faster.
Harvest push, building season | Faster at one kind of work.
Clean sweep | Cleaning 50% faster, and everyone who can clean does it before other work, after fires, the sick, children, prisoners and cooking.
Best behavior | Better negotiating, recruiting and trade prices.
On guard | Better aim and melee, more tiredness.
Austerity | No new wishes; standards fall fast.
Festival days | A big mood lift; work much slower; standards rise.
Days of mourning | Only while someone grieves. Grief fades much faster and mental breaks are less likely.
Quiet hours | Rest 15% faster in bed and far fewer social fights; work 5% slower.
Shared meals | Social impact up 10%, fewer social fights, some practice at talking every hour; work 3% slower.
Rest when ill | Wounds heal 20% faster and immunity builds faster; work 5% slower.
Banked fires | Fires, torches and fueled heaters burn 25% less fuel; work 4% slower.
Apprenticeships | Everyone practices construction, crafting, cooking and growing every hour; work 8% slower.
A feast day | One day: hunger 40% faster, work 15% slower, standards rise slightly.

Tithes | Each morning a tenth of the silver (5 to 40) goes to a people of the colony's ideoligion, or the nearest village: 1 goodwill a day, and with Ideology the faithful grow surer. Not for a tribe.
A curfew | Night hours (10 at night to 5) become sleep in everyone's schedule, put back after; night owls keep the watch. Far fewer social fights.
Militia drills | Twelve days of light practice at shooting and melee for everyone who can fight; work 3% slower. Not for a spacer colony.
Alms for the poor | Each morning a little raw food (5 to 20) goes out at the gate: 1 goodwill a day with the nearest friendly people.
Holy days | Ideology, a colony with an ideoligion: three days, the faithful 3% surer each day (half again with a chaplain) and a little steadier; work 8% slower.
A market day | A trade caravan of a friendly people comes the day it's declared; trade prices 4% better and work 5% slower for two days.
A fast | Two days: hunger 50% slower, learning 10% faster, work 6% slower.
A work song | Work 3% faster, and recreation every hour for those at work who don't mind it; research 10% and learning 5% slower.

Quarantine | Only while sickness goes round the region, or someone at home is ill: illness passes between roommates a fifth as often, visitor events come a third as often, immunity 6% faster; social impact down, work 4% slower.

Famine bread | Only while a famine, a drought or locusts lie over the region: hunger 15% slower at home, and a share of the raw food (6 to 24) goes each day to the hungry people of the famine, 2 goodwill a day.
Open gates | Visitor events come half again as often; social impact and negotiation up 5%.

One ideoligion for the colony | Ideology, more than one ideoligion at home: fifteen days naming the ideoligion you choose; everyone of another ideoligion leaning toward it a little more each day, a word from it at every council meeting, and those of other ideoligions trusting the council a little less each day. No mood of its own. "Ideoligions and the council" has the details.

li.after: Each decree also says something about the colony: long hours make it more hard-working, festivals more easygoing and traditional, being on guard more guarded.

li.heading: The everyday decrees
li.text:
The six newest decrees trade a few percent of work for something the colony needs, and their good moods are deliberately small. Quiet hours suit a tired or quarrelsome colony, but night owls hate them and the sociable mind losing their evenings. Shared meals help a colony full of newcomers get to know each other. Rest when ill pays off when several people are sick or hurt at once. Banked fires stretch the woodpile through a hard winter: the fuel is handed back to fires, torches and fueled heaters each hour, never to generators, to stoves while they cook, or to anything switched off. Apprenticeships spread the colony's trades so one fever can't leave it without a cook; they help the unskilled most, since practice counts for more at low levels. A feast day costs food and half a day's work for one day of good cheer.
Colonists petition for these when the moment fits: when someone is ill or many are hurt, in winter, or when someone new has joined. Anyone still healing from a wound or an illness likes resting when ill (unless they're industrious or tough) and a clean sweep (unless they're lazy), and asks for either when many are hurt.

li.heading: Decrees of a settled people
li.text:
The eleven newest decrees come from a village's own year, and do something no stat can: they give away silver and food and earn goodwill for it, send people to bed, call traders in, shut the gate or open it. Most of their good moods are small; the point is what they do.
Tithes and alms give a share of what's in store each morning (a quartermaster stretches it), and the news says where it went. A curfew turns everyone's night hours to sleep and puts them back exactly as they were when it ends (an hour you changed meanwhile is left as you set it); night owls keep the watch, and the sleepless are left alone. A market day only comes when a friendly people who send caravans is near enough; if none can come, the news says so. A work song's recreation only goes to those who don't mind the singing.
Some decrees only exist in the right colony: tithes are for a village, not a tribe, militia drills not for a spacer colony, holy days only with Ideology and an ideoligion of the colony's own. A decree that can never apply isn't listed at all. Two answer the region's hard times and can only be declared while one lasts: a quarantine while a sickness goes round (or someone at home is ill), famine bread while a famine, a drought or locusts lie over the region. Colonists petition for them when the moment fits: when the stores are full and the colony content, or when the world event they answer begins.
Who minds what goes by their nature, as with every decree, and with Ideology by their ideoligion too: the devout love holy days and approve of tithes, alms and a fast; those of another ideoligion mind holy days.

li.heading: When to call one
li.text:
Start rationing before winter, while there's still food to save, and run drills while raids are still small. Pair a hated decree with a short one people love, or follow it with festival days.
Colonists sometimes petition for a decree when the moment fits. Declaring it within five days wins their trust.

li.heading: Repeating and forcing
li.text:
Repeating a decree within 30 days makes it harder to bear. For each recent time, those against it lose more trust in the council and resent it 35% more while it lasts. A decree still on cooldown can be forced through, at a price: it counts as one more recent time, and those against it take it badly.
Each repeat can also make someone snap: a 20% chance per recent time, 15% more when forced, at most 80%. The hot-tempered throw a tantrum; others wander off in a daze.
So space out the decrees people hate. If you must repeat one, the tab shows how many times it was used this month, the chance someone snaps, and in how many days it's safe to enact again. Force a decree through only in an emergency, and keep the hot-tempered busy and away from the stores while it lasts.

li.heading: When it's needed and wanted
li.text:
A decree the colony needs now, and wants, can come again sooner and is minded less. It's needed when the moments it answers hold: those it's asked for in, and for a clean sweep and a sick bay the fighting too. Each counts a third, or two thirds when it's bad (food for under three days, a second big threat within ten days of the last, two grieving or ill, spirits very low, a filthy home, strain at 60, half the colony hurt). It's wanted as far as those who love or like it outnumber those against it, and more when someone has asked for it.
Needed and wanted, its rest after it ends is up to two thirds shorter, and those against it mind a repeat up to 60% less: less lost trust, less resentment while it lasts, a smaller chance someone snaps. Needed but wanted by nobody, a little of that. Wanted but not needed, none. However needed, a decree keeps at least a day and a third of its rest, and patience wears thin: once it has been declared twice in a month, the need counts for half. After fight on fight, with the home filthy and many hurt, a clean sweep that's asked for can come again in about four days instead of eight. The decree's card says when it's needed and why.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: dilemmas
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Hard choices where every answer costs someone something.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Whatever the council decides, someone at the table will hold it against them.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every week or so, more often while everyone is content, the council is asked to settle something: a thief, a feud, a stash, a feast, a confession, a duel, the spoils of a raid. A letter lists the answers. Colonists react according to their nature, and some answers are gambles. If you don't answer in time, the default answer is taken.

li.heading: Choosing an answer
li.text:
Some answers take real things from the stores: food, wood, silver. They're grayed out if you can't afford them.
Check the trust list first: a colonist who is already doubtful takes being overruled much harder. When kind colonists and hard ones are both present, the "fair" answer usually upsets the fewest people.

li.heading: Seasons and battles
li.text: Seasonal dilemmas (midsummer, harvest home, the longest night, naming the year) and after-battle ones (the spoils, the enemy dead, a victory feast) come up at their moment. Every dilemma and its answer is written into the chronicle and counted in the year's annals.

li.heading: Everyday life
li.text:
Many dilemmas grow out of what is happening to people right now. Someone ill when the medicine is down to a few doses; a fever that could spread through a shared room; a cook with a cold; an old family remedy, or a visitor's strange cure. A group camped on the colony's land asking for medicine, food or searchers for a lost child: how the colony answers changes how tense things are at their camp and what their people think of you. A council meeting someone missed while they were out working. A worn-out colonist (with feelings and strain on) asking for days off just when the harvest is in or the walls are broken. A squabble that grew into a feud, an elder who wants to put down the tools, a child with a question, a broken window, a child frightened after a raid or grieving, lessons for the children, two children fighting over a den, a youngster who wants to see the world, an old one who wants one last look at the hills, won't see the doctor, can't get warm, wants to tell the colony's story or to teach a little one, the old way against the new, a broken promise, the same meal or the same work every day, too many people in too little room.
Many answers call on whoever is best placed: the doctor, a forager, a tracker, a scholar, the best talker. They are grayed out when nobody fits, their skill makes a gamble less likely to go wrong, and the outcome names them. Medicine spent on someone eases their illness but never cures it outright, and no answer makes anyone sicker.
Health brings its own: a doctor who lost a patient asking for a day away, someone still convalescing who wants to be back at work (where going back too soon can make the recovery longer, never worse), family who want a say before an operation (putting it off suspends the operation until you resume it), and with Biotech, a midwife looking for an apprentice.

li.heading: What you'll see
li.text:
With "Answers play out on the map" on (the Events and world page of the settings, on by default), an answer that describes something people do happens on the map, and a message says when it starts and where. A victory feast is eaten at the dining table: everyone who comes is sent to eat a cooked meal from the stores, the finest first, and the message says so if there aren't enough meals for everyone. A bonfire is lit (if the colony has no campfire, one is laid in the open from its wood and burns down to ash afterwards), a toast is raised, the colony goes down to the water for the midsummer swim, an apology or a reading is heard round the table, a friend sits with someone who is ill, a colonist sits by a grave or walks over to the camp's fire, an apprentice works at the teacher's side, someone worn out gets the rest of the day off. Others send a few out as a work party to clean, haul, mend, build or bring in the harvest, walk the colony out to the graves or the gate, keep a vigil into the night, search the land for what was lost, carry a gift out to a visitor or hunt the game the answer marked (answers on the map has them all).
Nobody is called away from danger, sleep, a sickbed or someone else's care, and nothing starts while enemies are about: it waits a few hours for its moment (an evening feast waits for the evening). The good moods of the answer come to those who were there, once it's over. If it never happens, everyone it was for gets them anyway, as answers always did. Feasts eat real meals: keep a few cooked ones in the freezer when you say yes to one (Vanilla Cooking Expanded's grills spoiled by the cold are never served). A toast is raised with real drinks too, when the stores have them: beer or wine (Vanilla Brewing Expanded's included) for those whose drug policy and beliefs allow it, tea or coffee for teetotalers and the young, one each, never for anyone with a chemical addiction.
What each colonist is served fits what they believe and eat. It's only what their food policy allows (for a drink, their drug policy), nothing that would give them a bad "ate ..." memory (meat for a vegetarian, fungus for one who despises it, paste for one who finds it disgusting), and nothing Alpha Memes would make them sick for: for someone whose ideoligion holds both its fungus and its insect diets, only fungus, insect meat, insect jelly or a meal with some of either, never paste where paste is forbidden, never a simple meal where good food is expected. An ideoligion that frowns on drink gets tea or nothing at a toast. With nothing fit for them in the stores, they sit at the table and eat nothing, may write about it in their journal, and nobody counts it as the council forgetting their plate.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: names, anniversaries and annals
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How the colony remembers its people and its years.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Write the year down before people start remembering it differently.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Whoever has done the most of something earns a name for it (the Healer, Deadeye, the Kindling) until someone overtakes them. Each year since a colonist joined is marked. When a new year begins, the colony's best reader or talker writes the annals of the year that ended.

li.heading: Earning a name
li.text:
Names come from the colonist's records: wounds tended, operations, kills, headshots, things built, rock mined, harvests, sowing, repairs, meals, animals tamed, prisoners recruited and talked to, research, crafting, fires fought, patients pulled through, babies delivered, and less flattering ones like messes cleaned, things torn down, times on the operating table, times on fire or mental breaks. A name moves to someone else only when they're clearly ahead, by about 15%.
Rimfolk also counts a few deeds the game doesn't, and shows them in the Records tab: quarrels mended (the Mender), trade deals struck as negotiator (the Haggler), secrets other colonists trusted them with (the Vault) and eulogies given (the Mourner).

li.heading: Names from beyond the walls
li.text:
Some names are earned out in the world. Four more records count what a colonist does beyond the colony's own work: evenings spent at the fires of camps on the colony's land (Friend of the Road, from 10), camps met at the gate (the Gatekeeper, from 3), the colony's days kept by them on the calendar (Daykeeper, from 4) and world events' calls answered by them in person (Good Neighbor, from 3).
Others are given once, for one deed, and stay with their holder: the builder lent to raise the roofs of a burned town may be called Roof-Raiser, the one who carried the last of the blood price that ended a feud Feud-Breaker, the one who built the bridge after a war Bridge-Builder, the one who found a neighbor's lost child the Finder, and the one who walked an old pilgrim home Road-Warden.

li.heading: Names that come with time
li.text: Some names count years rather than deeds. The Old Hand has been here longest, two years at least. Homegrown spent the most of their childhood here. Jailbird spent longest in the cells before joining. Two have a condition: the Unshaken has lived here a year without a single mental break, and Lucky a year without taking any damage at all. Either name is lost the day that changes, and can't be earned back.

li.heading: Names from a seat, the ideoligion and the colony's years
li.text: Rimfolk counts a few more things in the Records tab, and names come of them. Each name shows somewhere in play.

table.li: Name | Earned by | Where it shows
Old Doc | two years in the physician's seat | sick travelers come asking for them by name
Old Iron | two years as marshal | villages that were raided come to ask how to hold out
The Unbeaten | three terms as speaker, and never a vote lost in any election | the election letter says so when they keep the chair
The Celebrant | leading six of the ideoligion's rituals to their end (Ideology) | neighbors come asking for a blessing
The Shepherd | two years as the ideoligion's moral guide (Ideology) | the doubting come to sit with them
The Founder | ten years here, as one of those who came in the first two days | the founding day's letter, their death letter
The Last of the First | being the only founder still here, of two or more, a year on | the founding day's letter, their death letter
The Firstborn | being the first child born here, now grown (Biotech) | the founding day's letter, their death letter
The Annalist | writing the annals three years running | they keep the pen, even if someone sharper arrives

li.after: Like every name, these count for a candidate in an election. A vote lost counts in an election for any single seat, so a speaker who once stood for marshal and lost is no longer unbeaten.

li.heading: The annals
li.text: The annals cover who joined, died, left or walked out, raids, wealth, wishes, ambitions, decrees, dilemmas, friendships, feuds, trust and names. Past years can be reread from the Chronicle page. At each anniversary of the landing a second letter comes, with the same setting: the year on the land and from beyond it, which the annals leave out. The herd (its head, who leads it and of which line, the young born, a new leader, one in its last season), the beast that stays, the neighbours settled for good and the loads that went down the road from their post, the camps that came, the faces that came back, the world events that ended and how, the allies, and a few lines of the year's chronicle about strangers and the world. The annalist writes it too.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: offices and elections
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Speaker, marshal, quartermaster, physician, steward, and for a bigger colony reeve, peacemaker, keeper of days, herdmaster, chaplain, warden of guests and a council of elders.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: The colony votes for the people it likes, not always the ones who are best at the job.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The council has five seats from the start, and more that open as the colony grows: seven more offices, one of them (the council of elders) with three seats. Each gives its holder a bonus and helps the whole colony in some way. Colonists elect them once a year, voting for whoever is good at the job, has the right nature for it, and is liked. The council can appoint or dismiss anyone from the Decrees page, but overruling the vote has a cost.

li.heading: The seats

table.li: Office | What it does
Speaker | Chairs every council meeting. Everyone's trust rises a little each day, at no cost to you.
Marshal | Drills train half again as fast, and the colony aims and strikes a little better.
Quartermaster | Answers to dilemmas that cost food, wood or silver cost a quarter less, and trade prices are better.
Physician | Everyone heals and fights off illness a little faster.
Steward | Standards rise a quarter more slowly, and the steward gets more out of recreation.
Reeve (4 voters) | Every harvest yields a little more (2%), and the reeve sows, reaps and harvests better still.
Peacemaker (5 voters) | Rivalries between colonists cool a little every day, and now and then the peacemaker sits the worst-feuding pair down, which eases their rivalry a good deal.
Keeper of days (6 voters) | Every council custom or calendar day the colony keeps leaves everyone there a small good memory (+2 for two days).
Herdmaster (6 voters) | Everyone gets a little more from milking, shearing and eggs, and the herdmaster tames and trains more easily.

Chaplain (5 voters, Ideology) | Keeps the colony's ideoligion: its decrees and customs strengthen certainty half again as much, and the chaplain is persuasive and steady. Only with Ideology and an ideoligion of the colony's own; those of the ideoligion count for a candidate, those of another against.
Warden of guests (5 voters) | Looks after visitors and the strangers camped on the colony's land; negotiates better and talks easily with strangers.
Elder (10 voters, three seats) | The council of elders. While any elder sits, the whole colony keeps a slightly steadier head. Age counts for a candidate.

li.after: A seat opens once the colony has that many people who can vote; until then it simply isn't contested. The election letter says a word about each new holder. The three elders' seats are elected one after another; the Decrees page lists each.

li.heading: Elections
li.text:
The first election comes after about a week, then one every new year. An empty seat is refilled by a by-election a few days later, as long as someone without a seat can take it. No one can hold two offices, and children, slaves and lodgers can't run.
Only those who can do a seat's work stand for it: someone incapable of medicine is never the physician, and a seat asks for some skill unless nobody who can hold it has more. The seats few people can fill are voted on first, so the colony's one doctor isn't spent on the speaker's chair, and a holder who can no longer do the work steps down. Among those who stand, votes follow skill, traits and friendship: friends and members of the same circle vote for each other, rivals against. Losing an election or a seat sours the loser on the winner, and can start a rivalry.
Overrule the vote only when the difference matters. The colonist who won the election will remember it.
Two more things weigh on a ballot. Someone whose granted wish the council took back in the last year holds it against everyone sitting on the council (about a third of a vote's worth). And the names the colony gave a candidate count for them, a dubious one against.

li.heading: In the colony's life
li.text: With "Systems talk to each other" on, the offices also do their jobs where you can see them:

table.li: Office | Also
Keeper of days | Organizes the calendar's feasts and games days (not the days about one person, which belong to them).
Peacemaker | Steps into a spat nearby, now and then: the two are sore at each other half as long.

Physician | Does the rounds of everyone convalescing each morning, taking about two thirds of a day off each recovery, and the office counts for two patients pulled through toward a doctor's good name.
Reeve | Deals with neighbors who ask the colony for goods; an order filled in full under the reeve brings 3 more goodwill.

Herdmaster | Sits with anyone whose named animal dies, and minds the animals of those away two days or more (they come home grateful). Goes down to name each newborn in the herd, brings word face to face to anyone whose animal is sick or hurt (their strain eases), and about once a week takes someone keen on animals, four levels or more behind, along for the day's work.
Marshal | After a fight at home, has a word with everyone who fought beside them, easing their strain.
Steward | At a gathering, eases the strain of everyone else there a little.
Chaplain | Most days sits with someone grieving (their strain eases) or has a word with the believer least sure of the ideoligion (6% surer); leads the calendar's remembrances.

Warden of guests | Spends an hour a day at the fire of any camp on the colony's land (its tension eases by 4, and the campers come to know the warden), and sees visitors welcomed: their people's goodwill rises by 2, once every few days for each people.
Elders | Every couple of days, each elder sits with someone ten years younger or more and passes on what they know best (an afternoon's practice in it), and the two grow a little closer.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: traditions
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What the colony keeps doing becomes expected.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Hold the midsummer feast two years running and they'll expect it every year after.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Some seasonal dilemmas have an answer the colony can make its own: a midsummer bonfire, a harvest celebration, a vigil on the longest night, a planting day in the fields. Choose the same answer two years running and it becomes a tradition. From then on it comes up first every year, keeping it pleases everyone, and breaking it disappoints them.

li.heading: The customs

table.li: Season | Custom | What it needs

Spring | The planting day: when the fields open after a cold season, the colony sows together (a work party) and the grower says a few words at the field's edge that evening; hope and practice, no mood. Let go, the growers (and the faithful of an ideoligion that holds nature dear) mind a little | land with a cold season, the first days the fields can grow again, 10 or more cells waiting for seed. Or name a planting day on the calendar
Spring | The remembrance walk: the colony visits its graves together and says the names | graves of the colony's own dead
Spring | Naming the year (the muffalo is a tradition too) | nothing
Summer | The midsummer bonfire | firewood
Summer | The midsummer swim: an afternoon in the water | a river, the coast or open water, and a hot day (22 °C or more)
Fall | Harvest home, a feast | raw food
Fall | The harvest dance: music and dancing, no feast | nothing but a late night
Fall or winter | First-frost soup: one big pot on the first freezing day | raw food, and the first frost
Winter | The midwinter supper on the longest night | raw food
Winter | Lantern night: a lantern in every window | firewood
After a raid | Burying the enemy dead, the victory feast | a raid
Any time | The remembrance night, for a fight two comrades want marked | comrades, raw food
Spring | A tree for every child, planted at the edge of the fields | a child (Biotech), a mild day
Summer | The children's race, with the colony cheering them round the fields | a child, a fine day
Fall | The children's gleaning: what's left in the stubble is theirs, shared at supper | a child
Winter | The snow day: no chores, everyone out in the snow | a child, a freezing day

li.after: The herd's year has customs of its own (the colony's animals has them): the lambing watch, shearing day, and bringing the herd home before the winter, in a cold snap or after a raid.

li.heading: Customs of the land and the ideoligion
li.text: Some customs only come where the land asks for them, and some only to a colony whose ideoligion keeps them (Ideology). Other mods' biomes count by their names: a mangrove is a swamp, a salt flat a desert. Nobody asks for a custom their own beliefs rule out: no fire customs from those whose ideoligion despises fire, no blessing from those who despise religion, and the ancestors' supper is served by the feast's own rules, each to what they may eat.

table.li: Season | Custom | What it needs
Spring | The sun's return: everyone round a fire on the high ground at dawn to see the sun come back | the tundra or the boreal forest, firewood
Spring or summer | The rain welcome: the whole colony out in the rain together (recreation, no mood) | a desert, and rain falling
Spring | The blessing of the waters: a loaf given to the water at the start of the year (trust, no mood) | the coast, a lake or a river, and open water
Summer | The marsh lights: the bounds walked after dark with smoking torches | a swamp or a jungle, a warm day, firewood
Fall | The high watch: the colony climbs the high ground to see all it has made (recreation and awe, no mood) | mountains or hills
Winter | The night vigil: the ideoligion's vigil through the longest night | Ideology: an ideoligion that worships (a theist or ancient one), someone devout to ask
Spring or summer | The tree-singing: the colony sings to the oldest tree (recreation and awe, no mood) | Ideology: an animist ideoligion, nature first, or tree connection
Fall or winter | The ancestors' supper: a place laid at the table for each of the colony's dead | Ideology: an ideoligion of the colony's own, graves of its dead, raw food

li.after: The ideoligion's customs strengthen the faithful's certainty, half again with a chaplain in office.

li.text:
The letter says when a choice is a tradition, and when choosing it again will make one. Keeping a tradition gives everyone a good memory; breaking one gives a bad one and resets the count. New, kept and broken traditions are written into the chronicle and the year's annals, and someone usually writes about a new tradition in their journal.
Traditions cost something every year, so only start the ones you can afford in a bad year too.
Days on the colony calendar grow into traditions the same way: keep one three years running (founding day, harvest day, a day you named) and the colony expects it. See "the colony calendar".

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: friends, rivals, comrades and mentors
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The bonds between colonists: how they form, grow, sour and end, and what they change.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Colonists who work side by side don't always end up friends.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists form lasting bonds out of how they feel about each other and what they go through. Steady liking turns into friendship, steady loathing into rivalry, fighting side by side into comradeship, and a skilled colonist may take an eager learner under their wing. Every bond has a strength and a short history, shown on the council's Bonds page and, for one colonist, in Rimfolk's column of their Social tab, beside the game's own list. Hovering someone in that list says what is between the two of them: a bond, a group they share, memories, views they agree or differ on.

li.heading: The four bonds

table.li: Bond | How it forms | How it ends
Friends | Two colonists' opinions of each other stay high enough. | It drifts with how they feel, and ends when it fades to nothing.
Rivals | Their opinions of each other stay low enough. | The same way as a friendship.

Comrades | Fighting in the same battle: drafted, manning a turret or attacking the enemy. Everyone who does becomes comrades. It is respect more than friendship, and adds a few points at most. | It slowly fades between battles.

Mentor and student | A mentor (skill 12+, with a passion) teaches a student (skill 7 or less, with a passion) each day the two spend some time side by side. | The student graduates at level 11 and goes to thank the mentor, and both are proud.

li.after: Bonds add opinion, more at each stage: new, solid, deep. To keep a skill in the colony after your best worker dies, look for a mentorship on the Bonds page, or have a learner with a passion work alongside them.

li.heading: How two people get on
li.text:
Time together doesn't make everyone friends. How two colonists get on follows the game's own compatibility between them, a fixed number for each pair that the game also uses for how often they have deep talks or trade insults, and that a big age gap lowers. Between two who don't click, a deep talk or chitchat counts for a third to two thirds as much, a slight stings a little more, Rimfolk's warm moments come up less often and frictions more. Between two who get on easily it goes the other way.
After five days side by side it shows in the Social tab, and deepens over a month as far as their compatibility goes: two who don't click (-3), rub each other the wrong way (-6) or get on each other's nerves (-10); two who are easy company (+3) or on the same wavelength (+6). Most pairs are in between, and what happens between them decides. Hovering someone in the Social tab says when two don't click or get on easily. Partners are left alone, and so is anyone outside the colony.

li.heading: What moves a bond
li.text:
Small social events happen most days, always between two who are together at the time: late talks, pranks, snubs, squabbles, war stories, lessons, contests, gifts, gossip and the odd truce. Life brings its own: a friend keeping vigil at a sickbed, an evening at a camp on the map, a quarrel over what the council decided, fears confided in the night, grief carried together, homesickness shared, a peace offering after a quarrel. Each moves the bond a little. Keep rivals on different work shifts to avoid squabbles.
The council's decisions feed back too. Losing an election to someone, having your wish passed over for theirs, a fight, a grudge from a dilemma or arguing over a decree can start rivalries. Backing the same petition, making up or going through something together builds friendships.

li.heading: Moments and frictions
li.text:
Smaller still are the moments colonists share in conversation, picked among the game's own chats: grieving together, talking shop, a story by the fire, a friendly contest. Who they are shapes them: night owls keep each other company in the small hours, undergrounders praise the rock overhead, brawlers compare scars, an iron-willed colonist steadies a nervous one, two gourmands plan a feast. So does what is going on: someone visits a sick friend or swears by an old remedy, two who spoke at the council talk it over afterward, the colony watches a camp's fires from the wall, and with the heart on a frightened colonist confides in a friend or a grateful one says thanks again. Frictions are the other side: chores, snoring, a borrowed knife, an annoying voice, a pyromaniac near the tinder, a nudist at the supper table, someone keeping their distance from the sick, a spat about the camp, a temper running high. Some only come when something real happened: a cook blamed by someone down with food poisoning, a bad day after a mental break turned into a joke, the proposer of a finished council project taking the credit, a shared tool handed back damaged. The home has its own nuisances, each read from the real map, so fixing the cause is the cure: a sticking door, a leaking roof, a cramped or smoky room, a generator by the bed, a filthy room, a cold or stifling one, an animal in the bed, building work next to it, vermin indoors, a bare earth floor, rotten food in the stores, rain with no coat when the colony could make one, junk left in a bedroom.
Moments, frictions and social events tell one story between the same two people. After a spat nothing warm passes between them until it wears off (usually half a day to a day, half as long again with an abrasive or volatile one of them, a day and a half after a falling-out) or one of them makes up, and a spat right after a warm moment is unlikely. A peace offering only comes after a quarrel.
Most warm moments change how the two see each other rather than anyone's mood: a joke or a story by the fire gives a little recreation, talking shop a little practice in a passion they share, and a child shown how to do something learns a bit of what the grown-up knows. Grief shared, a friend steadying someone in a bad hour or cheering them up when they're low still lifts the mood (see "Rising standards").

li.heading: Groups
li.text:
With "Personalities and social life" on, the colony's groups (see "Groups") have names, roles, habits and a history; they grow out of friendship, work, battles and more, and can split and merge. With it off, groups are simpler: three to six colonists held together by strong friendships, worked out afresh each day. Either way a group votes as a bloc, and colonists outside every group, with no close friend, sometimes feel left out.
Let someone's wish lapse and their close friends trust the council a little less, and those in the same group lose slightly more.

li.heading: What bonds change
li.text: Friends and members of the same group back each other's wishes and petitions and vote for each other; rivals object to each other's wishes and vote against each other. A colonist's bonds and circle are listed in their trust tooltip on the Wishes page. When a bonded colonist dies, the ones left behind write about it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: dreams
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What colonists dream about, and the rare dream that changes something or comes true.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: What a colonist dreams about is usually what's been bothering them.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A colonist who sleeps (or lies unconscious) for four hours or more may wake from a dream. Dreams grow out of their life: the battle two days ago, the friend they lost, the rival who insulted them, the wish the council ignored, the leg they no longer have, the skill they're learning. Most dreams leave a line in their journal and little else: a sweet dream a bit of rest, a strange one now and then an inspiration, a nightmare or a visit from the dead a passing mood. Hover over that mood in their Needs tab to read the dream itself.

li.heading: What they dream about
li.text:
Dreams about what really happened (a raid, a death, an insult, a broken promise, an illness, an addiction) are far more likely than others. People in their lives turn up: friends, rivals, partners, family, comrades, teachers and students, bonded animals, and the dead they loved.
Unhappy colonists have more nightmares, and volatile ones more still. Recurring nightmares usually mean a colonist is unhappy; check their Mood tab for the cause.

li.heading: What they feel, and what's around them
li.text:
With the heart turned on, feelings bring dreams of their own, likelier the stronger the feeling. A colonist angry at someone argues with them all night (and the rivalry grows a little); one grateful to someone repays the debt in a dream (and likes them a little more); envy dreams of someone else's life. Every one of the feelings has dreams of its own, grief and disgust among them.
Quirks bring dreams (a storm-dreader's storm, the dark for someone who sleeps with a light, the stars for a stargazer, the plants answering back), and so do life goals (a wedding for someone who wants to marry, the far road for a youngster who wants to travel, the last fine piece for an old maker) and personal stories (two doors for a rival in love, a rope pulled both ways for someone caught between two people, one more spring). Every habit and quirk has dreams of its own now, and so do nearly all life goals and personal stories: a book with no last page for one who reads at meals, a coat that mends itself for one who mends their own clothes, smoke under the door for a light sleeper, a long table for one who remembers every birthday, an answer from the dead for one who talks to them, an empty sickroom for a would-be healer, the council listening for someone who wants a seat, the master's bench for an apprentice, a small hand for a new parent, the animal at their side for someone raising an orphaned one. A dream for several quirks or goals has lines for each.
A nemesis comes back in dreams: standing at the gate while still out there (or, for someone feeling their resolve, faced at last), behind a locked door while in the colony's cells, and once it's over, gone from the dream as from the world. Someone whose family member or partner was killed by that enemy dreams of them too. Getting better and healing have dreams of their own: running again while convalescing (the impatient dream of the work waiting), a patient walking out of the sickroom, the empty bed after a loss, the first cry after a birth.
Ailments color dreams: a toothache brings dreams of loose teeth, a cold or a cough dreams of breathing underwater, insomnia dreams of lying awake, bites and rashes dreams of itching, a bad back or a kidney stone dreams of carrying a millstone, and getting over an illness dreams of being strong again. So does the world around them: a camp on the map, a council meeting they spoke at or missed, sickness, famine, fighting or a fair in the region (world events), and the time of year. The colony's own days leave dreams in the next night or two: gifts round the fire after a birthday, a day of gifts or a bonfire night, the day's sport after games, a hunt or a fair, a long morning after a day of rest, many hands after the planting day or a world event where the colony helped its neighbors. So does what the colony took part in out there: the warlord's fall, riders at night while a warlord is still loose (a rare nightmare), pilgrims' songs and peace made at the colony's table, wings over the fields after the locusts, the players after their evening or a camp's show, and the road home after a lost child, a pilgrim or refugees were seen safely on. A feeling and the world together dream deepest: fellowship by the camp's fire, the road with the camp for the restless, the fever at the door for someone worried while a sickness goes round, the open road for the hopeful in good times, gratitude for a camp's good turn and shame for a camp sent away.

li.heading: Dreams that change something
li.text: Now and then a dream leaves more than a mood behind:

points.li: an inspiration
a lesson in a skill
a good night's rest
a nightmare that leaves them shaken
a dream of a won fight that steadies their aim
a softened rivalry
a wish

li.heading: Omens
li.text:
Rarely, a dream is an omen, and a few days later it comes true: a caravan, a newcomer, falling cargo pods, a cold snap, a raid, or visitors following the lamp of someone who keeps one lit for travelers. Only one omen waits at a time. When a colonist wakes up talking about torches in the dark, check your defenses.
You can turn omens off with "Dreams that come true" in the settings.

li.heading: Telling them
li.text: Colonists tell each other their dreams, and telling someone you dreamt about them makes them like you a little more. Someone who keeps a dream book (a quirk, after a dream came true) dreams half again as often and writes every dream down. Recent dreams are listed on the Dreams page, and dreams that came true go in the chronicle and the year's annals.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: life goals
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What each colonist has set their heart on doing before they die.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A wish takes a few days to grant. A life goal can take years.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A few days after settling in, each colonist sets their heart on something: master a craft, marry for love, have a child, find three true friends, train a student, make peace with a rival, earn a seat on the council or a name the colony remembers, a bedroom fit for a noble, a warrior's or a builder's record, or simply to live three more years. Children have goals of their own (a best friend, a skill, their letters, an animal of their own, growing up) that grow into a grown-up's goal when they come of age, the young want to be taken seriously or to see past the hills, the old may want a grandchild, one more year or a last wish (a fine last piece, family set right), believers a role in their ideoligion or their faith found again, and some only want to feel at home, safe, loved or free of a grief. The Roster page shows everyone's goal and how close they are; the page "every life goal" lists them all.

li.heading: How a goal is chosen
li.text:
Goals fit the person: passions, traits, beliefs and situation decide what they want. A psychopath doesn't dream of true friends; an ascetic doesn't want a noble's bedroom; nobody whose ideoligion forbids lovin wants a child, and nobody whose ideoligion forbids violence wants a warrior's record. Someone whose ideoligion keeps lovin for the married, and who has a partner, sets their heart on marriage far more often.
Life sets them too. A battle can make a warrior, a brush with death a healer or someone who just wants more years, a wedding someone who wants to marry, a birth someone who wants a child, a lost election someone who wants a seat, and loneliness someone who wants friends. Seeing a friend achieve their goal can make them want the same. Something big can change their mind about a goal they've barely started.

li.heading: Getting there
li.text:
Once they're three quarters of the way there, they get a small, steady mood lift. Achieving it brings a letter, a long good mood (ten days, in full whatever their standards), a big jump in trust, and gladness among their friends, and it goes into the chronicle and the year's annals. And it leaves something behind.
That evening those close to them (family, a partner, anyone who thinks well of them) gather at the table for an hour, and the friend who thinks best of them raises a glass; they're glad of it, and so is everyone who drank. They're always inspired (unless they already are), in the way that fits the goal: surgery after a healer's, taming after a tamer's, recruiting after winning prisoners over, trade after other talk, creativity after a maker's, builder's or artist's, a shooting frenzy for a marksman, a go frenzy for a brawler, and a work frenzy for anything else.
The skill the goal was about (its own skill, or what it counted: meals for cooking, operations and births for medicine, enemies for whichever they fight with) is marked: it never slips again, and they learn it 15% faster. Goals reached before this came are marked too, and the Story tab says which skills they won't lose. Soon after, a younger colonist at home with a passion for that skill, and less of it, spends a couple of hours learning at their side, and both are glad of it. And the title stays: the Story tab remembers them as the one who did it ("cooked five hundred meals"), and the colony tells it round, so people bring it up in gossip.
After a while they may choose another goal, never the same one twice.
Check the Roster page now and then. A colonist one level short of mastery is worth a few days at their workbench. Goals like marriage, friends or peace with a rival can't be ordered, but shared work, shared rooms and shared battles help them along. Some dreams are about a colonist's goal, and some dilemmas come up because of one.

li.heading: Goals left unfinished
li.text:
A colonist who dies before reaching their goal is remembered for it: the chronicle notes what they never got to do, and their friends write about it. The person who loved them most may take the goal up and finish it for them. An old colonist's last wish left undone weighs on those who loved them for a week or so, and is likelier to be taken up, by anyone of any age.
Some goals cost something to give up: someone who never found love, a friend for life or their faith again feels it for a week when they let it go. A goal that belongs to an age grows up with them, or is outgrown.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: secrets, vendettas and eulogies
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What colonists hide, who they can't forgive, and how they say goodbye.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Not everyone talks about where they came from.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Some colonists carry a secret, often from the life their backstory hints at: a raider's past, noble blood, a deserter's shame, a child left behind, a borrowed name, an old illness, a debt to a trading house, a childhood in the camps, a broken vow, a hidden kindness. There are over sixty. You won't know what it is; the Bonds page only shows when they confide in a close friend, and the news of it gives a hint and no more.

li.heading: Confiding and coming out
li.text:
Confiding brings relief and brings them closer; it is done face to face, and if the two don't cross paths, the one with the secret goes to find the friend for a quiet word. A confidant who later becomes their rival is likely to let it slip, to whoever they are with; a close friend rarely does. Someone at rock bottom may blurt it out themselves, with someone there to hear it. So watch who confides in whom: if those two fall out, the secret will probably come out.
When a secret comes out, everyone reacts according to their nature: the kind forgive, the hard despise, the greedy envy, the abrasive mock. Betraying a confidence makes enemies. Some secrets put the council on the spot with a dilemma.
A secret the colonist never told anyone dies with them. If they told someone, it comes out at the graveside, each secret in its own way: a lamp left burning, a card in the grave, a name said aloud.

li.heading: Secrets from beyond the walls
li.text: A few secrets are born of what goes on out in the world, and only come while it does: medicine slipped to a neighbor's sick in a plague year, a verse given to the minstrels, bread left out for the exiles, a vow made under the comet, a letter given to the mourners for someone they'll pass, grain hidden under the floor in a famine or a drought, something seen at the market during a blood feud, a debt run up at a caravan's dice, letters sent off with a camp. While such a world event runs or such a camp is settled, one may come to a colonist it fits who keeps no secret yet, at most one a day. More than half of them are kindnesses, and come out as such.

li.heading: Vendettas
li.text:
When raiders kill or carry off someone, the people who loved them swear vengeance on that faction; when they kill a bonded animal in a fight, its person does. They carry it as a weight and fight harder when that faction shows up again.
A vendetta ends in one of several ways:

points.li: three of the enemy fall to the avenger, in the fights that come anyway;
some of them are taken alive in those fights instead: a captive counts as much as a death;
the one who was carried off comes home, by rescue, ransom or escape;
the avenger lays it down, after a month at least and not while the fighting is fresh. The kind do it sooner, the bloodthirsty and the cold never, and peace with the killers makes it much likelier;

the killers send the blood price (300 to 600 silver, more for a richer colony), 20 days or more after the oath, when no fight is on: the council can take it, leave it to the avenger (the bloodthirsty and the cold refuse, the kind accept, most others too) or refuse it;

once there's peace, an elder of the killers' people comes to say they are sorry: the avenger can accept it alone, the colony can hear it said in front of everyone and leave it to the avenger, or sorry changes nothing;
it lapses after two years, or when the faction is gone.

li.after:
An avenger who dies with the oath still open, while the colony is still at war with the killers, may leave it to an heir: blood kin first, then a partner, then a close friend, never one already sworn on the same people. The kind take it up less often, the bloodthirsty more. Otherwise it ends with them.
Those who swore vengeance take peace with the killers as a betrayal at first, though peace is also what lets most of them lay it down. Think twice before making peace with a faction that killed someone well loved, and give it time.

li.heading: Quirks
li.text: Colonists also pick up quirks from what they live through, at most two at a time:

points.li: a lucky helmet or weapon carried through a fight (good mood while it's on them, worn, in hand, as a sidearm or in their pack; bad without)
a dread of storms after a death
a battle ritual
night prayers after a dream came true
a fear of the dark after lying downed
grief that returns every winter
knocking on wood, after a fight or a fall: glad of it (+3) after a fight they came through unhurt
talking to the dead, after a loss: comforted (+2) near the graves
counting everything, after a dream came true or a secret came out: goes over the food stores in their free time, and tells you when the food won't last the week
salting the doorway, after a fight or a dream that came true: nightmares half as often
red is bad luck, after a bad fight (uneasy when wearing red)
checking the gate every night, after a fight
always cold, after a night spent freezing; watching the stars, after a night slept outside

li.after:
Most fade after a season or two. Each is a tag on the colonist's Story tab; hover it for how it came, what it does and how long it lasts (a quirk that does nothing to play says so).
A lucky thing says so: look at it on the map, open its info card or hover it in the gear tab, and it reads "Macy's lucky charm". It remembers, too. When the quirk fades or its owner dies, it becomes "Once Hector's lucky charm", for as long as the thing itself lasts, and a charm that has passed through several hands names them all.

li.heading: Habits
li.text: Habits come in their own ways. Most grow out of what someone does: Rimfolk notes once an hour what each colonist is doing (their kind of work, the hours before six in the morning, the hours after eleven at night, time out under the sky) and keeps about the last three weeks of it. A habit that grows out of work never comes out of the blue: without its work it doesn't come at all, and the more of it lately, the likelier, up to ten times its usual chance. A few habits are simply who someone is and come now and then to anyone they fit, whatever they do. A colonist holds two quirks at most, habits included.

table.li: Habit | Comes from | What it does | On the map
hums while working | working most of the day | work 2% faster | hums at work
talks to the plants | growing and cutting plants | plant work 3% faster | talks to the crops in their free time
names every animal | handling | taming and training 3% likelier | sits with the colony's animals
sings at the stove | cooking | 15% fewer food poisonings | sings while cooking
can't stand a mess | cleaning | cleaning 10% faster; -2 in a messy room | tidies up a dirty room in their free time
collects pretty stones | mining | +2 in their own room | looks for pretty stones
an early riser | being up before six | +2 in the morning, -1 up late | watches the sun come up
feeds the birds | time outdoors | +1 outdoors | feeds the birds
always whittling | crafting, smithing, tailoring, art | recreation drains 5% slower | whittles in a chair
steady hands | doctoring | tending quality +3% | looks in on the sick and wounded
measures twice | construction | builds 2% likelier to succeed | a word at the work
sharpens every blade | smithing | melee hits 2% likelier | sharpens a blade in a chair
knows every trail | hunting | hunting stealth +5% | watches the tree line
carries more than they should | hauling | carries 5 more | a word while hauling
keeps late hours | being up and busy after eleven | +2 at night | a word in the small hours
remembers every birthday | who they are (the kind and the sociable) | social impact +3% | seeks out whoever has a birthday, who is glad of it
talks in their sleep | who they are | a roommate -1, a lover +1 | mumbles in their sleep
saves the best bite for last | who they are | +2 for a few hours after a good meal | a word at meals
can't sit still | who they are | moves a little faster; -2 stuck in bed | a word when stuck in bed
reads at every meal | research | research 3% faster | a word over a page at meals
knows every prisoner by name | warden work | negotiation +3% | a word to a prisoner
mends their own clothes | tailoring | the worst-worn thing they wear mends a little each day | a word over a stitch
doodles in the margins | art (and anyone, now and then) | now and then inspired at their art, while they keep at it | a word over a doodle
sleeps light | putting out fires | wakes when fire breaks out near them or at home | a word up in the night
loves the snow | who they are | +3 while snow falls | stands out in the falling snow
follows the sun | time outdoors (never an undergrounder) | +3 out in the sunshine | sits in the sun
sleeps best in rain | who they are | +3 with rain on the roof, in bed or indoors at night | sleeps through it

li.after:
A habit with work behind it is lived on each day they're at that work enough, and any habit on each day they do its moment in their free time (with the small habits setting on). While it's lived it doesn't fade; once they stop, it lasts a couple of months more at least. Lived on sixty days (remembering birthdays: four birthdays remembered), it takes root: its knack and its good mood grow a little (cleaning 15% faster instead of 10%, say), the colony hears of it, and once they stop it lasts four months more at least. Lived on longer still, it can become a trait for good (see "traits that change").
Habits also pass between people who spend their days together. Each day a colonist may pick up a habit of someone close to them on the same map: a child from a parent, a student from their mentor, a lover, family by blood, a good friend they think well of. The closer they are, the likelier: a parent's habit reaches their child in a season or two, a friend's takes a year or more, and a habit that has taken root passes a little more readily. A habit that comes only from its work passes only to someone who does a fair share of that work too, and nothing passes that doesn't suit them. The habit's line says whom they had it from, and from then on it's theirs like any other. Grief, fear and lucky things don't pass; most habits and the small superstitions do. At most one a month each, and never past their two quirks.
A watcher of the stars, the dread of storms and the other quirks born of something that happened come as they always did; one who loves the rain (Weather is kinda cozy) never comes to dread storms.

li.heading: Quirks from what the colony lives through
li.text: Some quirks come from what happens to the colony out in the world and at home, within a few days of it, and fade after a season or a year. Each shows on the map now and then, as a word over their head when it fits what they're doing.

table.li: Quirk | Comes from | What it does | On the map

keeps a lamp lit for travelers | refugees seen through, a guest's thanks or a watch kept for one, being taken in, pilgrims fed, a good turn on the road, a pilgrim escorted home | friendly visitors and caravans who stay the night leave on better terms: +1 goodwill a visit | a word about the lamp at night

can't stand the smell of smoke | seeing the pyre beyond the gate burn, awake and within 40 cells of it (never a pyromaniac) | -2 within a few steps of an open fire: a fire, a campfire, a hearth, a brazier or a torch | a word near the fire
counts every coin twice | swindled, conned, cheated by a trader or haggling badly | trade prices +2% | a word over the silver
walks the fields at dawn | locusts, a lost crop, crops raided by animals | harvest yield +3% (+5% once rooted, kept while they keep growing) | a word in the fields in the morning
keeps a dream book | a dream of theirs came true | dreams half again as often, and every dream goes in their journal | a word over the book after a dream
swears by a healer's salve | a camp's healer, the famous healer or a traveling healer saw to them, or they watched the famous healer at work | wounds heal 10% faster | a word in the sickbed
juggles at supper | the players' evening, or a camp's show | eating or resting beside others in the same room, each of them has a little recreation (once in eight hours) | a word while juggling
swears by a trick against the cold | a traveler's trick against the cold, out in the frozen lands | comfortable 3 °C colder | a word out in the frost

li.after: All but the smoke and the dream book pass between people close to each other, like the habits. Each has dreams of its own, and the lamp keeper's can come true: visitors follow the lamp a few days later.

li.heading: Quirks in people's lives
li.text: Some quirks change how someone answers and speaks, and ask for moments of their own:

points.li: speaks in proverbs (the old): a saying at council meetings, in the answers to dilemmas and in the journal; it helps some people and grates on others
tells the old stories (from making peace in one more spring, or telling the colony's story): story hours with any children the colony has
sleeps with a light burning (a child after nightmares or bad nights): a small comfort in their own room, and a roommate kept awake
laughs at the wrong moments: at supper apologies, at sad stories, and at a graveside, which a grieving friend won't forgive quickly
a worrier (after a death in the colony or far away): lies awake late, checks the bolts with a friend, may ask the council for a night watch
writes everything down (scholars): reads back what was said, may ask to keep the colony's record
first to volunteer (kind or hard-working): takes someone else's turn at the worst job
a soft spot for strays (animal lovers): feeds every stray, with another animal lover

li.after: Each of these, and every other quirk and habit, has dreams of its own (a storm-dreader's storm, the stargazer's stars, a coat that mends itself, a long table, smoke under the door).

li.heading: Coming of age
li.text: With children (Biotech), coming of age is marked: parents are proud, the colony remembers the child they were, and the council is asked to help choose a path, often an apprenticeship that starts a real mentorship with the colony's best.

li.heading: After a death
li.text:
Half a day or so after someone dies, the person closest to them speaks at the grave. What they say depends on who the dead were: their years here, the name they earned, the goal they never reached, who killed them.
A dead colonist's weapon or hat passes to the person who loved them most. Carrying it is a comfort (to anyone, more to the heir), and losing it hurts.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: strangers, beasts and pets
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Visitors, traders, prisoners, fallen enemies, nemeses, wild animals and the colony's own animals.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A raider who gets away may come back with the next raid.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists don't only deal with each other. While visitors, a trade caravan, guests or prisoners are around, and every day among the colony's animals and the wildlife, small moments happen: news from the road, haggling, words through a cell door, a fallen raider's plea, a pet's mischief, a stag at dawn. Most of these give something other than mood: a herd going by or a clear night is a little recreation, a traveler's trick against the cold some comfort, an animal calmed in a storm practice, a traveler's star names a little research, a great beast awe and sometimes an inspiration, and the smallest only a line in the journal. Some put a hard choice to the council. And an enemy who badly hurts one of yours and gets away becomes that colonist's nemesis.

li.heading: Visitors and prisoners
li.text:
Encounters happen a few times a day at most, and never during a fight. Visitors and traders make them likelier while they're here. Warm moments make visitors like the colonist (their opinion of them rises), sometimes improve goodwill with their people, and count toward the "known far and wide" life goal. Let your most sociable colonists host visitors: good impressions add up to goodwill, and sometimes to a new recruit.
With prisoners, kind words soften them (less resistance); taunts and cruelty sour moods on both sides.
Council choices about strangers come with short deadlines when the stranger is only passing through: a visitor who wants to stay, a trader who wants an heirloom, beggars at the gate, a wounded raider who's still breathing.

li.heading: Nemeses
li.text:
A nemesis is an enemy who struck down, maimed or killed a colonist and lived. A raider who flees is remembered, and may ride with the next raid from their people. A wild animal that mauls someone and slinks off gets a name and keeps prowling.
Capturing a nemesis, or seeing them dead, lifts the mood of the one they hurt. Doing it by their own hand lifts them most, and completes the "settle the score" life goal.
A raider who gets away often has a parting word, and one who comes back usually has something to shout across the field; a beast leaves signs instead.
