The story can also end with the nemesis joining the colony, wearing its collar, being tamed, dying out in the world, vanishing, or being let go from the cells, which the one they hurt will have feelings about.
The one they hurt dreams of them (at the gate, behind the cell door, and once it's over, gone), and a fight at home can leave them bad nights. Two personal stories grow out of a nemesis: a fear faced while the enemy is still out there, and the fear laid to rest once they're in the cells or gone for good. The day a nemesis first came back, and the day one fell, go on the colony's calendar.

points.li: When a nemesis returns, put the one they hurt somewhere safe, or somewhere they can finish it themselves. Either way, expect a big swing in their mood.
Capture fallen raiders who downed your people: a nemesis in your cells can't come back with the next raid.
Hunt a named beast as a group. It already beat one of you.

li.heading: The colony's animals
li.text:
An animal that fights beside its person in a battle is remembered for it, the more so if its person was hurt and it stood over them. A named animal that dies gets a farewell from the one who loved it, shaped by how long it was here, how big it was and whether it died fighting. A bonded animal killed by raiders is a reason for its person to swear a vendetta on them.
What colonists want for their animals, the stories and dilemmas that come of them, the herdmaster's part and the herd's year are on the page "the colony's animals".

li.heading: The land, the seasons and the weather
li.text:
Some moments only happen in their place or their hour. In the desert a wild animal shares the noon shade; on the tundra and in the northern forest there are tracks in the snow and travelers with tricks against the cold; in jungle and swamp, eyes in the undergrowth, a cape of leaves in the rain, lights over the marsh at night; in the mountains, an animal on the ridge and news of the high passes; on the coast, the tide line and the sea in a storm, the wrack after it, the rock pools and a coast knot; by a lake, mist on the water at dawn, an animal crossing the winter ice and a traveler's night lines; by a river, the ford, first light at the water and an animal stranded when the river runs high. Spring brings the first green, fall the creatures getting ready for winter and the first frost, and rain, fog, snow, thunder and a clear night each have moments of their own; rarer ones come with the sky that makes them: an aurora, an eclipse, a falling star or a moon story with a traveler, heat lightning on a hot summer evening, eyes in the night fog, and with Odyssey an animal sheltering from a blizzard.
Rimfolk reads the land from the biome's name and the map tile (hills, mountains, a coast, a river), so the biomes other mods add count too: a mod's mangrove is a swamp. The everyday encounters have lines for each kind of land as well.

li.heading: Strangers from your other mods
li.text: Some moments only come with a mod that brings the stranger: Hospitality's guests talk about their room and their home and may ask to stay, visitors of the Empire or of Vanilla Expanded's republics and settlers talk about their own people, traveling mages and fighters of A RimWorld of Magic share a working or a form, and Alpha Animals' creatures are met by name, as are Odyssey's and Vanilla Animals Expanded's water birds, shore creatures and river creatures, ReGrowth: Extinct Animals' dodos and mammoths, and Stagz Merfolk's merren by the water. With Medieval Overhaul, visitors notice the colony's cheese, wine, hearth and books once it has them. The Almanac page "What Rimfolk does with your mods" lists what's in your game.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: the colony's character
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How the council's choices add up to a reputation: merciful or harsh, generous or thrifty, and more.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Turn away enough beggars and word gets around.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every answer to a dilemma, every decree and many granted wishes say something about who the colony is. Lean far enough one way and word spreads: the colony becomes known as merciful, thrifty, hard-working or guarded, and later renowned for it. Colonists are proud of ways that suit their nature and chafe at ways that don't. The "Our ways" page in the council window shows where the colony stands, who is proud, who chafes, and what shaped it.

li.heading: The five ways

table.li: Way | Who likes it
Merciful or harsh | Kind colonists like mercy; the bloodthirsty and psychopaths like harshness.
Generous or thrifty | Kind colonists like generosity; the greedy like thrift.
Traditional or restless | The old like tradition; the young like change.
Open or guarded | Sociable people like openness.
Hard-working or easygoing | The industrious like hard work; the lazy like ease.

li.after: Colonists whose nature fits the colony's ways get up to +4 mood; those whose nature clashes get up to -4. Decide what kind of colony you want to be, and let the council's answers follow: a colony that sticks to its ways keeps the colonists who share them happy. Check "Our ways" before recruiting, since a kind recruit will chafe in a harsh colony.

li.heading: Earning and losing a name
li.text:
Each way runs from -100 to 100. The colony is known for a way at 25 and renowned at 60, and loses the name a little below that. An answer given by default, when the council didn't decide in time, counts half.
Old deeds slowly fade, so a colony can change its name: about half of a way is forgotten in a year, and the further the colony already leans, the less each new deed adds. To change it on purpose, choose the other way for a while.

li.heading: With the neighbors
li.text:
A generous or open colony slowly gains goodwill with its neighbors as word gets around; a thrifty or guarded one slowly loses a little. Being open and generous is a slow, cheap way to keep neighbors friendly.
Some encounters and dilemmas only come up for a colony with a certain name: refugees seeking a merciful colony, traders who heard you count every grain.

li.heading: What the work makes a colony
li.text: Beside the five ways, a colony grows into what its people keep doing, counted from their own records as a rolling daily average per head over about forty days. Steady work for a season earns the name, and a letter says so; it fades if the work stops for long, though one winter alone won't undo a farming colony.

table.li: Known as | Earned by | Proud of it
Green-fingered | sowing and harvesting | those with a passion for growing
Builders | building | those with a passion for construction
Learned | research | those with a passion for intellectual work
Craftsfolk | crafting | those with a passion for crafting
Hunters | game brought down | those with a passion for shooting
Delvers | rock mined | those with a passion for mining

li.after: The proud get a small lasting mood (+2) while the name holds. The "Our ways" page shows how close the colony is to each.

li.heading: What the colony grows into beyond its work
li.text: More names come from how the colony lives with others, with its ideoligion and with its own years, and from what visitors see of it. They are counted for the colony as a whole from Rimfolk's own records, give nobody a mood, and change what comes to the colony instead.

table.li: Known as | Earned by | What changes

Good hosts | camps that stayed their time and left on good terms; visitors, refugees, feasts, guests of note and peace talks the region remembers; with Hospitality, guests staying the night | camps come a third sooner after the last; refugee families and exiles seek the colony out

Devout (Ideology) | the ideoligion's rituals held to their end, a chaplain in the seat, a moral guide in the ideoligion | pilgrims, processions and penitents come twice as often, and pilgrimages and holy years find the colony

Long-memoried | calendar days kept two years running or more, and traditions (three between them) | players, minstrels and mourners come twice as often, and a great death in the region is told to the colony first
Famed hall | visitors who remarked on a great hall, often enough over the months | tourists, the celebrity, the players and guests of note come more often
Artful | visitors who remarked on the art | tourists, the celebrity, scholars and scribes come more often
Hallowed | visitors who remarked on the graves | pilgrims come more often
Walled | visitors who remarked on the walls and the guns | tourists come more often

li.after: Each has its own visitors on the road (a word about the colony's warm fire, a pilgrim's prayer that steadies someone in their ideoligion, a stranger asking about the old days who teaches the teller to tell it well), and lines in letters that know the colony's name. And each leans the colony's old hands, those here a year or more: in a colony of good hosts they mind an answer that turns people away, in a devout or long-memoried one an answer that sets the old ways aside. Like the work names, these fade if the colony stops living up to them.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: reading moods
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The Mood tab and the Moods page: what weighs on your colonists, why, and what to do about it.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Most bad moods come from something you can build: a table, a light, a bed.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every colonist has a Mood tab next to their Needs: each mood with its size, why it's there, when it fades, which mod it comes from, and what you can do about it, sorted by what you can do. The council window's Moods page adds up every mood in the colony, so you can see what weighs on everyone at once, who feels it, and who is closest to breaking.

li.heading: The Mood tab
li.text:
The mood bar shows where a colonist is, where their mood is heading, and the lines below which minor, major and extreme breaks become possible. Under it, one sentence says how close they are to a break.
The tab sorts their moods by what you can do about them. A row of chips gives each group's total ("You can fix -15", "Will pass -11 · 2 days", "Ideoligion -4", "Lifting +22"); click a chip to jump to its group. Each mood is one line: a faint bar for its size, the number, its name, and on the right a short action ("Build a dining table") or when it ends. Hover a line for everything about it (the game's description, why, when it fades, what helps); click it to open its card in place, with buttons that lead to the advisor's matching warning, the council page that deals with it, or an Almanac page. Only one card is open at a time.
"Details" in the tab's header shows every mood as a card instead, the way the tab used to look; "Compact" goes back. Rimfolk remembers which you chose.
When a colonist has it good, a "Good times" line under the moods says how much Rimfolk's balance takes off their good moods right now: good moods that add up slowly, good memories that fade sooner, and comforts that high standards make count for less. Hover it for the rules. "Where it comes from" splits the mood between the base game, Rimfolk and each of your other mods, so you can see which mod is pushing hardest. The heart section (strain, feelings and the heart's needs) comes last, folded; click its heading to open it.
Click a group's heading to fold it away; it stays folded until you quit. Above a tall inspect pane, as with RimHUD, the tab gets shorter and scrolls.

li.heading: The four groups
li.text: Every mood goes in one of four groups, each in order of size, biggest first.

table.li: Group|What's in it|What the line says

You can fix|Moods you can do something about now: a mood that lasts while its cause does, or a memory that comes straight back until you act (a meal without a table, a night in the barracks)|What to do, in gold

Will pass|Memories that only fade (grief, a council answer, a story gone badly), and moods that end with what caused them (a world event)|When it's gone; the group's heading says when the last of them is
Ideoligion and who they are|Moods from their beliefs, their traits or genes, and moods that never fade|What their ideoligion asks, or "Their nature", or "Lasting"
Lifting|The good moods, folded to one line until you click it|When it ends

li.after:
A belief or a trait that asks for something you can build still counts as something you can fix: the altar their ideoligion wants, the bedroom a greedy colonist expects.
Moods from other mods are sorted by what kind of mood they are, with a short line to match: "While it lasts" for a mood that stays while its cause does, "Fades in 2 days" for a memory, "Their ideoligion" for a belief's mood, "Lasting" for one that never fades. Their card gives general advice and their mod's name.
The game's own Needs tab gets a line above its mood list with the same totals; click it to open the Mood tab. Hovering a mood there ends its tooltip with what helps.

li.heading: The Moods page
li.text:
The Moods page sorts the colony's moods into the same groups, one line per kind of mood with how many colonists have it; click a line for its card, with who feels it most. Start at the top of "You can fix": the biggest totals usually have the cheapest fixes, like a dining table, lights or a bedroom. Check "Closest to breaking" before a long job or a caravan, and give the shakiest colonists something good first.
A colonist sinking toward a break line needs help now: a fine meal, recreation, a party or rest, while you fix the cause.

li.heading: Setbacks
li.text: Rimfolk's bad moods come from something that happened, never from nowhere: the council's decisions, frictions between people, everyday pressures, and setbacks in the colony's life (work wrecked, a crop lost, a sick friend, long quiet days). Each names its cause in its tooltip, and the Mood tab says what helps. The Almanac's setbacks page lists them all.

li.heading: What colonists fix themselves
li.text: They tidy their room, visit a grave, take a break when worn down, or plan a cheap light, plant pot, passive cooler or sleeping spot for their own room. You get a message each time.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: Rimfolk events
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What comes to the colony from outside: pasts catching up, challenges, old enemies, the land and the sky, visitors with a purpose.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Sooner or later, someone from a colonist's old life comes looking for them.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every few days something comes to the colony from outside: an old comrade asks for a colonist by name, a traveling champion wants a contest, a comet hangs in the sky, mourners come to a grave. These are Rimfolk's own events. They join your storyteller's own random events and follow its rhythm, or, if you prefer, come on Rimfolk's own timer (a setting). The bigger happenings across the whole region are world events, with a page of their own. Many ask the council what to do; the answer shapes the colony's character, and often a colonist's life. Answer the letters: an unanswered one falls to a default, which is rarely the best choice.

li.heading: Pasts that catch up
li.text:
Who a colonist used to be (read from their backstory: soldier, outlaw, noble, trader, healer, scholar, farmer, artisan) decides which pasts can catch up with them. Bounty hunters only come for someone with a violent past. A colonist known by an epithet may be sought out by name.
A colonist who walked out or was banished may come back one day. A prisoner who dies in the colony's hands may be avenged by their people.

li.heading: Visitors
li.text:
Strangers who ask to join wait at the edge of the map until you answer. Use "Look at" in the letter to see who they are before you decide. Visitors, finds and inheritances fit the colony's era: a medieval colony meets medieval folk and digs up medieval things.
Contests with a traveling champion never hurt anyone: target shooting, wrestling without weapons, crafts, cooking, art, debate. The better one usually wins, and the letter says how good each side is, so read the odds before betting.
A traveling doctor's shots (or a herbalist's tonic) help everyone fight off sickness faster for a month. With answers playing out on the map, the doctor goes round the colonists and gives each their dose in turn (someone up and about stands still for it a moment), and a tinker paid to mend works through the worn clothes and weapons one at a time, where each lies in the stores or on whoever wears it; the answer's words come when the last is done, or a word says how far they got if they had to go first. A guest taken in for the night sleeps in a warm corner of one of the colony's rooms (never a bedroom, a sickroom or a cell), a traveling cook given the kitchen cooks the feast at the colony's own stove, and food, a coat or bandages an answer gives a visitor are carried out to them from the stores. What a journalist or chronicler writes depends on the colony's character: mercy, generosity and openness make for a kind article, and their opposites for an unkind one.

li.heading: Hail, vermin and the great beast
li.text:
Hail only hurts crops out in the open. Vermin only get into food that isn't kept cold, and a cat or dog may catch them first. Roof a field or two and keep food cold, and most of the harm is gone.
The great beast is tougher than any of its kind. It leaves in a few days, and only fights if provoked. If you hunt it, hunt with a group, not a lone colonist.

li.heading: Orders, debts and waiting
li.text:
A neighbor's order is collected five days after you take it. Only goods in your stockpiles and shelves count, and it's the whole amount or nothing. Some answers take days to come back, like a caravan to a far market, a cart sent to a harvest fair, a relative on the way or a guest who wrote ahead.
The council window's World page shows each of these and when it's due, along with fights on their way, questions waiting for an answer, and who's out there with the colony on their mind.
Keep some silver in the stores. Debts, bounties, tribute and treasure maps all ask for it.

li.heading: Fights
li.text: Fights only come if the settings allow Rimfolk events that can end in a fight, only when the storyteller sends threats at all, never on top of another fight, and at a share of the storyteller's own raid strength. Everyday events (stranded merchants, a tinker, a neighbors' quarrel, an old grave, a family visit, a fortune teller and others) never end in a fight. A band of the people someone swore vengeance on can be drawn into a fight at home, if you want it. A war band moving through the valley, or a family burned out of their farm by raiders, can bring a fight too, but only as the risk of an answer: keep watch on the walls, pay the neighbors' militia to turn the war band, or shelter the family and hope they weren't followed.

li.heading: Events that remember
li.text:
Some events follow from earlier ones: a deserter's old unit, a lost child come back grown, a rematch with a champion, the great beast's young, grateful pilgrims. A neighbor whose order you filled may come back to buy again, the runaway lovers' family may come asking after them, a relative who visited may write (and can be invited to stay), and neighbors remember how you judged their quarrel. The colony's founding day comes once a year.
The end of a world event can bring its people back about it, depending on how it ended and what the colony did: thanks after a plague, the first harvest shared after a famine, a flooded town's search for what the water took, spring seed and hands from those the colony sheltered through a hard winter, seed grain from old friends after locusts or a drought, and a reckoning after a hard year the colony looked away from. A people some colonist swore vengeance on may send the blood price, or, once there's peace, an apology. And a people that remembers one of the colony by name asks for that colonist: their visitors stop that colonist to say thank you, their traders may give them a friend's price, their envoys ask for them at the gate, and their letters say so.

li.heading: The land, the season and the era
li.text: Some events only come where and when they fit: a flush of mushrooms after rain in a mild, wet place, white nights near the poles in summer, a desert in bloom after rare rain, the long rains where it's hot and wet, an ice fair on a frozen river, the first snow, the longest night of winter, an eclipse. Callers fit the colony's era: a tribal colony may get a spirit singer, a medieval one a scribe, an industrial or spacer one a photographer or a tourist.

li.heading: Hard turns, and the neighbors' troubles
li.text:
Some events are hard on purpose. A killing frost gives a day's warning: send every hand to the fields and the ripe crop comes in before the cold, send a few for the best of it, or let it take what it takes. Something at the pens comes back night after night until someone sits up with a lamp or the herd is brought in, and only comes for a colony with a herd of three or more. Word of a death far away asks how the colony helps its own: a wake that evening, a day to themselves, or straight back to work, which is the hardest of the three. A colonist called home can say no, send silver instead, or go, seen to the gate by the others; someone who goes may come back one day as someone who left.
The neighbors bring theirs to the gate: a herd that needs the colony's river in a dry summer (the drovers bring the animals down to the water, and can cut wood while they drink), a fire on the far ridge that drives the game across the colony's land, a beast of theirs that strayed into the colony's barn, goods offered too cheap to be honest, a keepsake from a colonist's old life on a trader's blanket, a gambler, hired hands who fell trees for a meal, and a teacher for the colony's children. What the colony does is remembered: a herd watered or a stray returned counts as a good turn, a gate kept shut as a refusal.

li.heading: Callers who touch the colony's life
li.text:
Some callers only come when there's something for them to do. A bonesetter comes while someone is nursing an everyday ailment, and can ease it or cure it. A fiddler comes while someone is strained, and an evening of music takes some of the strain off. Guests who want to watch a council meeting come only once meetings are on. A peacemaker comes for two colonists who can't stand each other. A camp nearby can bring a shared feast, or a quarrel to settle.
Many answers call on someone with the right skill or trait: a good cook, a healer, a builder, a crafter who can teach. The letter names who it would be once you choose; when nobody at home fits, the answer is greyed out and says why.

li.heading: Stories in stages
li.text:
A few events are the first stage of a longer story told over days or weeks: a door in the hill, a fugitive at night, a feud in a nearby town, a preacher on the road, a lost expedition, a bundle of lost letters, a stranger's seeds, a play written about the colony, an apprentice from a nearby town, a traveler with a fever. The colony's answer, and luck settled when it matters, decide which stage comes next and when. The World page shows what's coming, and each story ends in one of several ways, written into the chronicle.
The last two run over a whole season. The apprentice comes up from their town a day or two each week to learn at the bench of the colony's best crafter, makes a first piece and a journeyman's piece that are really handed over, and somewhere in the middle there is trouble (a guild that wants them, homesickness, or bad company at the market): how the colony meets it decides whether they stay, go home a journeyman, or drift away. The traveler with the fever is nursed through the night by the colony's best doctor (it counts toward the hospital's name), may come back when the fever does, and returns well, to work off the debt or stay. Later the same fever reaches their town, and they come back to ask for medicine: what the colony did at the start decides how that ends.

li.heading: Missions
li.text:
Now and then a neighbor asks for something done by a deadline: tame a runaway prize animal, raise a shrine for pilgrims, supply a funeral or a wedding, help a town rebuild after a fire, a storm or a flood (wood, stone blocks or more wood, cloth, and steel or components for an industrial town), or send provisions for a hard winter, a dry year or a sickhouse (raw food or pemmican, meals, medicine, cloth, firewood). Only goods in your stockpiles count. All of it pays well over its worth; at least half pays its plain worth; less, and they go elsewhere and think less of the colony.
The peoples that think best of the colony ask for other things: guests at their feast or a wedding (a caravan to their town), an apprentice for one of their masters, a bedroom fit for a guest of rank, or food and a roof for refugees for a few days. Friendly peoples also ask the colony to walk an old pilgrim home by caravan, to carry word to a far town of another people, to find a child of theirs lost on the colony's land before nightfall of the second day, or to send hands for their harvest in summer or fall. Each remembers the colonist who did it, by name. The page on what the world remembers has the details.

li.heading: With other mods
li.text: A few events only come with certain mods.

table.li: Mod | Event
A RimWorld of Magic | Lights falling from the sky
Alpha Animals | A strange creature
Dubs Bad Hygiene | Travelers asking for a bath
Hospitality | A guest of note who judges your guest room

li.heading: What you'll see
li.text: With "Answers play out on the map" on, many answers happen on the map too: the colony gathers round a fire for the spirit singer, at the camp's fire when the camp holds a feast, out in the open for the photograph, the drumming at an eclipse or the birds coming back, round the table for the founding feast or a letter read aloud; a colonist sits with a visitor or a stranger who asked for them, sits by a grave, or works at a traveling teacher's side for the afternoon; the colony gathers for the players' play or a storyteller's tales, walks out in the evening to a fallen star, sets a quarreling pair to rebuild the woodpile together, sends a picker out for mushrooms, carries bread out for travelers on the road, and the hunters go after a beast. Newer answers show too: the colony out in the fields bringing in the crop before a frost, a watch walking the pens or the walls until dawn, a neighbor's herd drinking at the river with a colonist on the bank, logs lying where hired hands or a mended traveler felled the trees, a doctor sitting up at a feverish traveler's side, a wake for someone who died far away, the colony seeing someone off at the gate, and an apprentice's piece collected from beside them and carried in to the table. Answers on the map says how it works and when it waits.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: scenarios with stakes
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Rimfolk's scenarios start the game with something already in motion: a friend on the way, a mentorship, an enemy, a debt, a feud, a prisoner, a council, a secret, children to raise.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Not every colony starts with a clean slate.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Rimfolk adds seventeen scenarios, marked "(Rimfolk)" on the scenario page along with how hard they are. Eight are gentle starts with no attacks of their own: four small ones with one or two colonists (The Inheritance, Master and Apprentice, Runaway Hearts, The Lone Hunter), three for a small company (The Players' Cart, The Quiet House, The Homestead) and The Orphanage (with Biotech). Nine come with stakes (Hot Money, Marooned, Deserters, Bad Blood, Borrowed Time, The Fallen Tyrant, The Elders' Fire, What the Ship Carried, The Land Grant). A few seconds into the game a letter says how things stand. Their pieces are scenario parts you can add to any scenario in the editor.

table.li: Scenario | What to know
Hot Money | Decide early whether you're keeping the silver. Spending it and then refusing to pay it back is the worst of both.
Marooned | Someone in the pods is lying. Keep the friendships strong and the truth will come out sooner.
Bad Blood | Friendships across the two families matter most. Shared work, shared meals and a common enemy all help.
Borrowed Time | Trade from day one. Half the debt paid on time buys three weeks.
The Fallen Tyrant | The tyrant is out cold for the first few hours. Build a cell with a bed before the drug wears off.
The Players' Cart | Four players and a muffalo. Visiting performers come first, then a fair or a talent scout. One of the company isn't who they say they are.

The Quiet House | Three of a quiet order, a mentor and a novice among them, known from the start as merciful, generous and traditional. Pilgrims and holy folk come soon after; one of the three broke a vow once.
The Homestead | A married couple and an old friend, with cows, chickens and seed potatoes. Family visits or writes within the month, and a buyer or a fair comes after the first harvest.

The Elders' Fire | Five of a tribe. The eldest who can holds the elder's seat from the first day, and two of the tribe's days are traditions from the first year: keep them, or the colony feels it. A neighboring people's war band comes twice for the old feud, and one of you has sworn vengeance on them (three of theirs to fall) with a life goal to match.

What the Ship Carried | Three survivors and one secret, carried by one and known by all three. It can only come out to people who join later, when one of the three lets it slip, so friendships with newcomers cut both ways. The wreck comes down as a world event two or three weeks in, with salvagers, cheap steel and maybe pirates.

The Orphanage | Biotech only; without it the scenario isn't there. Two carers and three or four children, all fond of each other from the start, and one carer has set their heart on seeing a child grown. Nobody comes to attack; a storyteller, players or a lost child come instead.

The Land Grant | A medieval holding: the colony counts as one of the old ways until it researches past them, and the lord's reeve comes asking for a tithe. The speaker, the marshal and the reeve are named in the charter and sit until the year turns. The lord's people remember the grant as a debt, and in time ask for it back as a favour: answer kindly and the debt is settled.

li.heading: Sworn enemies and hunts
li.text:
A sworn enemy is a nemesis from the first day. If their people hunt the colony, they come a set number of times, a month or so apart. The hunt ends sooner if that enemy dies, joins the colony or is sold off, or if their people make peace or are wiped out.
The "Fights in Rimfolk's scenarios" setting makes those attacks weaker or stronger, and your storyteller's difficulty scales them too. Fights a scenario promises come even with Rimfolk events that can end in a fight switched off, but only when the storyteller sends threats at all.

li.heading: Debts
li.text: A debt comes due as a letter with three answers:

points.li: Pay it.
Pay half and ask for more time. The rest grows by about a third, and they only wait twice.
Refuse, and meet the collectors.

li.after: Unanswered, a debt counts as refused. Debts and hunts are on the World page.

li.heading: Feuds and arrivals
li.text:
Two feuding families each take one surname. Family members like each other more, and dislike the other family; the grudge fades over a couple of months if nothing feeds it.
Someone from the past, a visiting scholar or a great beast arriving "around a set day" waits for a quiet moment. If they can't come yet (the wrong season, nobody fits), they try again the next day.

li.heading: Councils, customs and debts from the start
li.text: The newer parts set up more of the colony's life before it begins:

points.li: A council already formed: seats filled before anyone votes, by the eldest who can (an elder) or by whoever is best at the work. This year's election counts as held; empty seats still get their by-election.
Days the colony keeps: days brought from the old home, on the calendar as traditions from the first year. Kept here two years running, they help the colony become long-memoried.
A life goal from before: for whoever swore vengeance, keeps the secret, is eldest, or looks after the children.
Beholden to a people: the colony holds its land by their grant. They remember it as a debt (on the World page) and call it in as a favour some weeks later.
Children in the colony's care (Biotech): children who arrive with the colonists, with nobody else.
A world event set in motion: one starts around a set day if it can, and waits for a quiet moment. Not with world events switched off.

li.after: A secret can be shared: one carries it and every grown-up who came knows it, so only those who join later can hear it let slip. A sworn enemy can be a neighboring people of the old ways, with a vendetta sworn against them.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: feelings and strain
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Strain wears colonists down over days; feelings color their wishes, dreams and moments; four needs show what their life is missing.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A high mood doesn't mean someone is fine. Check their strain after a hard week.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
Mood says how a colonist feels today. Strain, from 0 to 100, says how worn down they are: it builds slowly from fighting, pain, losses and bad nights, and comfort can't buy it off quickly. Alongside it, each colonist has one or two feelings at a time (grief, fear, pride, joy and others) and four long-term needs of the heart.
None of this changes how the game decides on mental breaks. Vanilla mood stays the number that counts. Strain reaches the game only through one mood of its own, a small slowdown at work, darker dreams and, at the very end of the rope, a day off; feelings and needs never add mood at all.

li.heading: What builds strain

table.li: Source | How much
Fighting | 4 an hour while drafted or attacked with enemies on the map (12 a day at most)
Pain and serious injuries | up to 6 a day
Being downed | 3 an hour (8 a day at most)
Deaths and losses | 4 for a colonist's death, 5 for seeing an ally die, 8 for family, each memory once (14 a day at most)
Long days without sleep, no free time | up to 4 and 3 a day
Bad nights (cold, heat, noise, outside, on the ground) | 1 or 2 for each, once a night (4 a day at most)
A dark home (under a roof, not the night sky), hunger, very low mood | up to 2, 4 and 6 a day
Hard council decisions | decrees they resent (1 to 3 a day) and dilemma outcomes that hurt (4 a day at most)
Fear, grief, worry and despair | up to 2 or 3 a day while they last
A need of the heart badly lacking (below 25) for about three days | 1 to 2 a day for each such need (3 a day at most)

li.after: Everything together adds at most about 25 a day. Iron-willed colonists take 40% less and steadfast ones 20% less; nervous ones take 25% more and volatile ones 40% more. Psychopaths take nothing from deaths, the bloodthirsty little from fighting, masochists nothing from pain. The strength setting makes all of it build from 50% to 150% as fast.

li.heading: What drains it
li.text:
Strain drains by itself in quiet hours (0.15 an hour), faster asleep in a bed at a comfortable temperature (0.6 an hour, 0.25 elsewhere) and during recreation (0.5 an hour). A good mood speeds this up by a quarter, a very good one by half. Joy, pride, hope and calm speed it further; despair and dread slow it. When all four needs of the heart are at 60 or more, it drains 20% faster.
Some things take a chunk off at once: a party (6), a concert or a wedding (5), a festival, feast or celebration (3 to 8, 12 a day at most), a deep talk or a good moment with a friend (1.5 to 3, 6 a day at most), and a good cry (catharsis, 30). A colonist with a warm bed, free time and a decent mood sheds about 10 a day, so one hard day takes two or three to undo.

table.li: Strain | Band | What it does
0 to 29 | Steady | Nothing
30 to 54 | Strained | -3 mood, darker dreams
55 to 74 | Worn down | -5 mood, 5% slower work, more nightmares
75 to 100 | Near breaking | -8 mood, 10% slower work, many nightmares; from 85, a day off may come

li.heading: A day off
li.text:
At strain 85 or more, a colonist may simply stop: they keep to their room for six to twelve hours, eating and sleeping as they need, and do no work. A letter says why and what would help. It never happens in danger, while drafted or asleep, while hurt or sick, in the middle of caring for or carrying someone or fighting a fire, to children, slaves, prisoners or guests, or when fewer than two others could keep working; at most once in 2 days in the colony and once in 10 days for each colonist. It ends early if a threat appears, if they need a doctor, or if their room gets too cold or too hot. Afterwards their strain drops by about 40 (20 if it was cut short) and they feel lighter for a day and a half (+6 mood).
To head it off, use days of rest: a decree that slows everyone's work by 10% for three days and makes strain drain about twice as fast. Colonists may ask for it when the colony is worn down.

li.heading: Feelings
li.text: Feelings come from the moods a colonist has right now (as big as the game counts them) and from what they can see: enemies on the map, a fight on its way, a new face, quiet days. The strongest one or two show in the inspector; the Mood tab lists every one they have, how strong, since when and why. They add no mood, because that would count the same thing twice. Instead they nudge: a wish that fits becomes up to half again as likely, moments between colonists go warmer or pricklier, dreams change color, strain builds or drains faster. Each nudge is at its fullest only when the feeling is strong.

table.li: Feeling | Comes from | Nudges
Grief | deaths and losses | a grave for the dead, grief shared, dreams of the dead, some strain
Fear | danger here and now | defenses and weapons, nightmares, strain
Dread | what's coming: a promised fight, a warband, a lean winter | stores, medicine and defenses, a trickle of strain
Anger | insults, fights, unfair decisions, a rival, strangers camped on our land, a warlord who got away | frictions, wishes for justice
Shame | a prisoner executed or sold, a break they regret, a camp driven off, neighbors turned away in a hard year | fewer warm moments, wishes that make amends
Envy | someone else's room or things, the council's favorite | frictions with them, the same things
Disgust | raw food, corpses, rot, filth | a clean colony, better food
Loneliness | no friends here, a partner away, left out, a friend gone on with the camp | warm moments, a party, a companion
Homesickness | new here, family elsewhere | good food, keepsakes, dreams of home
Frustration | refusals, lapsed wishes, work they love turned off, crops lost to the locusts, a prize lost at the fair | less patience, frictions
Despair | long low spirits, loss after loss, a colony losing | slower recovery, a day off likelier
Joy | good meals, parties, wishes granted | faster recovery, warm moments, sweet dreams
Pride | good work, victories, a seat, a name, a prize at the region's fair, a peace made at our table, neighbors helped | faster recovery, art and fine things
Love | a partner or children close by | warm moments, sweet dreams, less loneliness
Gratitude | rescued, tended, helped, a wish granted, a camp's good turn, a famous healer's cure, a stranger's blessing | warm moments with the one who helped, trust in the council
Hope | spring, a newcomer, healing, strain lifting, good news from the region (a fair, a new road, a peace) | faster recovery, less despair
Awe | auroras, eclipses, the comet, beautiful things, pilgrims singing in the night | art, flowers, a shrine, very rarely an inspiration
Contentment | quiet days with needs met | faster recovery
Curiosity | research, books, visitors and camps, new land, a master healer at work, a pilgrim's road | books, lessons, journeys
Restlessness | the same work every day, too little fun | time outside, travel, a hunt
Nostalgia | anniversaries, old stories, an heirloom, long years here, old age | a memorial, a hearth, dreams of the lost
Relief | a fight survived, a hunt or debt over, someone brought home, the warlord fallen or the warband broken up | faster recovery, less fear, a day off
Tenderness | a baby, a patient, a little one learning, a bonded animal, a lost child seen home | warm moments, less anger, a crib or a pet bed
Worry | someone loved downed, ill, carried off or away; a sickness in the region for parents and healers, hunger in the region for growers | a sickbed visit, an infirmary, a trickle of strain
Fellowship | feasts and customs kept together, a group, friends close by, friends made at a camp, good neighbors to a camp, its music at night | warm moments, less loneliness, parties and music
Resolve | a score to settle, drills, a steady nerve, a goal half won | less despair, fewer episodes, training and weapons

li.after: The world beyond the walls reaches the heart too: what passes between the colony and a camp or a neighbor feeds the feelings above, and while a camp is on the map or a world event runs, a feeling that fits brings dreams and moments of its own (the camp's fire in a dream, friends at the camp talked about, worries about the region shared with a friend, plans made on good news, a camp sent away regretted).

li.heading: The heart's needs

table.li: Need | Met by | Makes likelier
Belonging | friends here, a partner, family, a group, good moments | parties, companions, a wedding; goals about friends and family
Purpose | work they love, a life goal, a seat, learning | a space for their craft, lessons; goals of mastery
Safety | no danger, food, medicine, defenses, their health | defenses, armor, an infirmary; goals of a fighter
Freedom | time outdoors, free time, varied work, travel, few restrictions | time outside, travel, a hunt; goals of discovery

li.after: Each runs from 0 to 100 and is worked out every hour from what their life has now; none gives mood. What each one does is in the next section.

li.heading: What the heart's needs do
li.text: The heart's needs never add or take mood. They change what a colonist wants, what they feel and, if a lack goes on for days, how worn down they get. Hover any of them (the inspector line, the Mood tab, RimHUD, the council's tables) to see the value, what raises it and holds it down right now, what follows from it and what would help.

table.li: Value | What it means | What follows
60 or more | Well met | With all four here, strain drains 20% faster
45 to 59 | Fair | Nothing yet
Below 45 | Missed | The one they lack most makes the wishes that answer it up to 35% likelier and life goals up to half again as likely

Below 35 | Low | It deepens its feeling: little belonging makes them lonelier, little freedom more restless, little safety more uneasy, little purpose more frustrated (by up to 3, about half of what makes a feeling felt)
Below 25 | Badly lacking | After about three days, it adds 1 to 2 strain a day (3 a day at most for all of them) until it rises again

li.after: The three days are counted by the hour: an hour below 25 adds one, a better hour takes two away, so one good evening in a lonely week only pauses it, and a few good days undo it. A slave's freedom never adds strain this way; that is what being a slave is, and the game weighs it already. Purpose never falls below 25 (a life always has some), so it nudges and colors feelings but never wears. Most often it's belonging that runs that low, for a newcomer with no friends yet or someone left out, and freedom, for someone kept indoors with no free time.

li.heading: Where to see it
li.text:
The Mood tab has a Heart section: the strain meter with its band, what built it lately, what would help, every feeling and the four needs (hover each for what it means). The council's Moods page lists who is worn down. A short line in the inspector reads like "Strain: worn down · restless, proud · lacks belonging" (the need shows while one is missed); hover it for the whole story. RimHUD can show strain, feelings and needs. Hover the strain mood in the Needs tab to see what built it up.
Settings, on the Heart & health page: feelings and strain on or off, the day off, the inspector line, and how quickly strain builds.
